bill_description: S.2, the Secure America Act, is a bill in the U.S. Congress. This description uses the Senate-engrossed version, meaning the version the Senate passed, with text dated June 5, 2026. The question is what would change if the bill took effect on June 9, 2026, compared with the law in force on that date. The bill gives about $70 billion more to federal agencies, in addition to money they already have. The money can be used until September 30, 2029. It goes mainly to Customs and Border Protection (CBP), the agency that guards the borders and includes the Border Patrol, and to Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), the agency that arrests, holds and deports (“removes”) noncitizens. Some money goes to Homeland Security Investigations (HSI), the part of ICE that investigates crimes, for work other than immigration and customs enforcement. The bill pays for officers and staff, detention and deportation operations, border technology, and other enforcement work.

claims.title: General HSI money reaching human trafficking investigations

claims.classification_reason: The reported reassignment of existing HSI staff is a concrete challenge to this assignment step. The legal spending limit cuts the other way. Reports do not show where new hires would work. Other HSI assignments are separate propositions.
claims.scope_html: This concerns only this kind of work and the general Section 102 money. It excludes the reserved child-exploitation funding. The question is whether added capacity reaches this work; how much is a later question.
claims.background_html: Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) is the part of ICE that investigates crimes. Section 102 tells ICE that this money “shall be used for functions other than those related to Homeland Security Investigations' immigration enforcement and customs enforcement missions.” [1]
claims.support_html: The legal limit keeps this money away from immigration and customs work: it must be used “for functions other than” those missions. [1] HSI has done this other work in the past, including cases about trafficking, fraud and cyberattacks. [18]
claims.objection_html: Senators reported in January 2026 that “entire HSI units have reportedly been reassigned” [21] to immigration enforcement. Cato reported in September 2025 that HSI “is suspending investigations into human trafficking, child exploitation, cybercrime” [23]. Section 202 separately pays staff in “all its directorates” [1] to do immigration enforcement. So the legal limit controls how this money is spent, but it does not decide where other staff are assigned. These are reports about staff who already worked at HSI. They do not show where Section 102 hires would work, and they do not show that the money cannot reach this work.

arguments.title: Better-supported border patrols can reduce pollution of water that wildlife uses.
arguments.pro_html:
Point 1 Better-supported border patrols can reduce pollution of water that wildlife uses.

  • Because The Department of the Interior manages many federal lands. It reported that border staff and equipment reduced damaging traffic: “By deploying personnel, equipment, and infrastructure, CBP operations have reduced cross-border illegal activity and the environmental impacts of this illegal activity in a number of areas.” [2] CBP is Customs and Border Protection, the federal border agency.
  • Because The Forest Service said that people crossing the border leave trash behind: “Perhaps one of the most well known of the impacts of illegal immigration is the litter left behind” [3].
  • Because This trash can ruin water that wild animals drink: “Water sources near this contamination are often so fouled by pollution that wildlife can no longer use them.” [3]
  • So Section 201 pays for staff, and Section 103 pays for surveillance. Both support patrols like the ones Interior describes. Where added patrols reduce crossings through wild areas, they can reduce this pollution. Protecting water that wildlife uses serves [NAME]'s care for nature.
arguments.con_html:
Response These local gains do not show that S.2's added patrols would reduce this traffic instead of moving it somewhere else.

  • Because Interior reported gains in some places: “CBP operations have reduced cross-border illegal activity and the environmental impacts of this illegal activity in a number of areas.” [2]
  • Because The Forest Service reported that stronger controls beside Coronado National Forest “funneled growing amounts of illegal vehicle and foot traffic through the valleys and mountains of the Forest.” [3] “Funneled” means pushed into one place.
  • So Enforcement can reduce traffic in one place and push it into wild land in another. So one step is missing: that added patrols would reduce the traffic near wildlife water, and not only move it.

arguments.title: Catching people faster protects habitat from damaging traffic and broken livestock fences.
arguments.pro_html:
Point 2 Catching people faster protects habitat from damaging traffic and broken livestock fences.

  • Because Section 103 pays for towers on the southwest and northern borders only if CBP (Customs and Border Protection, the federal border agency) has tested and accepted them “to deliver autonomous capabilities.” [1] “Autonomous” means the system works without constant human control.
  • Because CBP reported that people were caught faster with autonomous towers: “The response time from target identification to suspect apprehension dramatically decreased,” [4]
  • Because The Forest Service reported that “unauthorized trails and roads have been created on the Forest by illegal foot and vehicle traffic.” [3] It said that when these trails spread, this “damages and destroys cactus and other sensitive vegetation; disrupts or prohibits revegetation; disturbs wildlife, their security and travel routes; causes soil compaction and erosion” [3].
  • Because Crossing traffic also broke a fence that protected the habitat (home area) of endangered species. The fence became “ineffective in restricting livestock use” [3]. As a result, “This fence damage has allowed the destruction of endangered species habitat to continue” [3].
  • So Paying for staff and faster detection makes it easier to stop damaging traffic and fence damage. That protects plants, wildlife habitat and soil from destruction, which [NAME] values.
arguments.con_html:

  • So Keeping a person from running away before a timely removal can justify custody even when the person is not dangerous. This argument does not show that monitoring would serve that purpose in the cases it objects to. So its step from “no safety threat” to “unjust confinement” leaves out that question.

arguments.title: It adds capacity for enforcement that targets people by ethnic or national background.
arguments.pro_html:
Point 1 It adds capacity for enforcement that targets people by ethnic or national background.

  • Because S.2 pays for staff and operations of Customs and Border Protection (CBP) “in order to carry out immigration enforcement activities.” [1]
  • Because Human Rights Watch documented tactics by ICE (Immigration and Customs Enforcement) and CBP in Los Angeles in summer 2025 that included “detaining people based on their perceived race, ethnicity, or national origin” [14].
  • So Human Rights Watch says the package moves “without adopting essential oversight and accountability reforms.” [14] More capacity for these operations, without those reforms, increases the risk of this documented practice of treating groups as suspects.
  • So Accepting different ethnic and national groups gives [NAME] a reason to oppose added support for treating people's background as a reason for suspicion.
arguments.con_html:
Response This argument does not connect the added staff to more ethnic profiling under the conditions in place at the vote. Ethnic profiling means treating people as suspects because of their ethnic group.

  • Because The investigation describes a particular campaign “throughout the summer of 2025 in Los Angeles” [14]. The relevant question is about added work after June 9, 2026.
  • Because Before the vote, CBS reported a change in Border Patrol's street operations, according to Tom Homan, a top administration official on border policy: “He noted that, since the Minneapolis operation was scaled back, Border Patrol agents have not been making seemingly random immigration stops at parking lots and public places.” [15]
  • So This argument projects the earlier campaign's methods onto added staff without addressing this later change. So more enforcement capacity alone does not establish more use of that particular way of choosing people. This is an official's account, and it does not show that such stops have ended.

arguments.title: It pays for separating established immigrant neighbors from their families and communities.
arguments.pro_html:
Point 2 It pays for separating established immigrant neighbors from their families and communities.

  • Because S.2 pays for “transportation costs and related costs associated with alien departure or removal operations.” [1] “Removal” means deportation.
  • Because A report published before the vote found: “Individuals who are not public safety threats and have deep ties to their communities have been indiscriminately targeted under this administration.” [16] It also records children experiencing “family separation as a result of a parent being detained.” [16]
  • Because The bill sets aside “Not less than $350,000,000” [1] for certain immigration arrest and custody work, including “custodial transfer, release monitoring, transportation, and arrests of covered unlawful aliens” [1].
  • Because Some adults qualify without a conviction: “following an arrest, charge, booking, or conviction for a criminal offense under Federal, State, or local law, other than a minor traffic offense, is the subject of an immigration detainer, notice request, or custody-transfer request issued by the Department of Homeland Security” [1]. A detainer is a government request to hold a person for immigration officers.
  • Because This arrest fund cannot pay for release or community alternatives unless existing law requires it: “None of the funds appropriated pursuant to this paragraph may be used, except as required by existing law, to release, parole, place on alternatives to detention” [1].
  • So The added deportation money and the arrest fund's preference for custody strengthen the means of separating people from community life, including parents and people without convictions.
  • So Accepting different people as neighbors gives [NAME] a reason to oppose more ability to exclude the established community members described above, who are not threats.
arguments.con_html:
Response Separation from family and having no conviction do not by themselves show rejection of people for being different.

  • Because The transport provision pays for “alien departure or removal operations.” [1] Removal is a civil process tied to immigration status, not a criminal punishment: “deportation is classified as a civil rather than a criminal sanction” [17].
  • Because The arrest fund includes an adult who, “following an arrest, charge, booking, or conviction for a criminal offense under Federal, State, or local law, other than a minor traffic offense, is the subject of an immigration detainer, notice request, or custody-transfer request issued by the Department of Homeland Security” [1]. These conditions concern criminal process and immigration custody. They are not tests of ethnicity, faith or opinion.
  • Because The limit on release spending applies to “funds appropriated pursuant to this paragraph” [1] and keeps the exception “except as required by existing law” [1]. It does not cancel release rights or stop other money from paying for release.
  • So This argument identifies family disruption and a preference for custody. Neither one makes acceptance of a person's background or beliefs depend on that person staying. The missing value step is why enforcing these civil rules rejects difference. Having no conviction does not supply that step.

arguments.title: It expands the police role that leads Latino residents to withdraw from contact and community life.
arguments.pro_html:
Point 3 It expands the police role that leads Latino residents to withdraw from contact and community life.

  • Because S.2 pays for “expanding, facilitating, and implementing agreements under section 287(g)” [1]. These are “agreements that allow state and local law enforcement agencies to perform certain immigration enforcement functions” [18].
  • Because A 2012 survey of Latinos in four counties found that people were reluctant to contact police “specifically because they fear that police officers will inquire about the immigration status of themselves, their friends, or their family members.” [19]
  • Because The same survey found: “Many Latinos feel isolated and admit to withdrawing from their community.” [19]
  • Because Recent reporting also describes this withdrawal. In March 2025, CalMatters reported a volunteer's account that “some families have refused to leave the house for fear of apprehension by immigration enforcement agents.” [20]
  • So Expanding the immigration role of local police strengthens a reason residents give for avoiding contact. The harm reaches beyond people who are detained: fear keeps other neighbors apart.
  • So [NAME]'s wish to listen to and understand different people gives a reason to oppose this added barrier to everyday contact.
arguments.con_html:
Response The evidence does not connect the added withdrawal to the local police roles that these agreements create.

  • Because The survey is about police involvement in general, in 2012. Its measure includes the statement “I feel more isolated because local law enforcement is more involved in immigration enforcement” [19].
  • Because These agreements cover different kinds of work. ICE (Immigration and Customs Enforcement) describes its Warrant Service Officer model as allowing local officers “to execute civil immigration warrants on behalf of ERO.” [21] ERO is ICE's enforcement branch. This model concerns warrants for people already in custody, not new street questioning.
  • Because The recent article concerns federal raids and rumors, including times when “volunteers show up to a report of a raid, only to find the rumors were prank calls.” [20] It also reports: “The sheriff has previously insisted in a video message that his office does not enforce federal immigration law.” [20]
  • So An account of fear in a place where the sheriff says he does not do this work does not show the effect of these agreements. This argument does not say which added police contacts would create the barrier. This response does not answer the survey's general finding about police involvement.

paths.original_excerpt: [NAME]'s wish to listen to and understand different people gives a reason to oppose this added barrier to everyday contact.
paths.necessity_reason: The barrier depends on which local police role the agreements create.

Keeps the real limits: other agreement types, and a recent article about federal raids where the sheriff disclaims this role.

arguments.title: It gives more legal help to the side seeking deportation while immigrants face barriers to telling their own story.
arguments.pro_html:
Point 4 It gives more legal help to the side seeking deportation while immigrants face barriers to telling their own story.

  • Because S.2 pays for government lawyers “to represent the Department in immigration enforcement and removal proceedings.” [1] A removal proceeding is the legal process that decides whether a person must leave the United States.
  • Because The American Immigration Council explains the existing imbalance: “Yet, in every immigration case, the government is represented by a trained attorney who can argue for deportation, regardless of whether the immigrant is represented.” [17]
  • Because The same report explains why detention makes it harder for an immigrant to answer: “Attorneys must adhere to strict visitation rules, making it difficult for lawyers to communicate with their clients.” [17]
  • Because A detention inspection described before the vote found “no way for detainees to contact their families and lawyers.” [16]
  • So The bill directs added legal help toward the case for deportation in a system where people in custody face documented barriers to presenting their own case.
  • So [NAME]'s wish to hear and understand those people gives a reason to oppose this spending priority.
arguments.con_html:
Response Paying for government lawyers does not by itself show a choice against hearing immigrants' circumstances.

  • Because Listening to someone's circumstances does not require agreeing that the person should win a legal case.
  • Because The report places immigrants' communication barriers in detention: “Attorneys must adhere to strict visitation rules, making it difficult for lawyers to communicate with their clients.” [17] This does not describe an effect of hiring government lawyers.
  • Because The government's lawyer does not decide whose story wins. The same report explains: “If the Notice to Appear does not state a valid ground for removal, the judge must terminate the case.” [17]
  • So This argument shows that immigrants need legal help. It does not show that paying for the other side rejects their account or blocks it. The unequal spending becomes an argument about tolerance only by assuming that support for the government's case works against listening to immigrants.

arguments.title: It pays for operations with a record of using force against peaceful opponents and people reporting on them.
arguments.pro_html:
Point 5 It pays for operations with a record of using force against peaceful opponents and people reporting on them.

  • Because S.2 pays for “operations and maintenance for its immigration enforcement functions.” [1] This is money for ICE (Immigration and Customs Enforcement).
  • Because In October 2025, Human Rights Watch documented “excessive force against peaceful protesters, legal observers, volunteer street medics, and journalists” [22] outside a detention center in Broadview, Illinois.
  • Because Its findings rest on witnesses and video: “Witnesses and video confirm that DHS agents used tear gas and fired projectiles directly into groups of protesters, including from the detention facility roof, often without warning, and without protesters appearing to pose any risk to agents.” [22] DHS is the Department of Homeland Security.
  • So Human Rights Watch says the package moves “without adopting essential oversight and accountability reforms.” [14] Added operating money without those reforms supports enforcement with a documented pattern of frightening peaceful critics and people who help others hear their views.
  • So Accepting people who disagree gives [NAME] a reason to oppose added support for this intimidation.
arguments.con_html:
Response This argument's prediction of more intimidation leaves out changes in the operations and command behind these confrontations.

  • Because Human Rights Watch tied the rising tension at Broadview to Operation Midway Blitz and “an increase in immigration raids and seizures throughout the Chicago area.” [22]
  • Because Before the vote, CBS reported: “Earlier this year, Mr. Trump charged Homan with winding down the Minneapolis operation after the fatal shootings of U.S. citizens Alex Pretti and Renee Good by federal immigration agents sparked intense, bipartisan backlash.” [15]
  • Because CBS also reported a change in the command behind the city sweeps: “Bovino was relieved of his command following Pretti's killing and retired from Border Patrol in March.” [15]
  • So This argument uses confrontations during an earlier approach to predict the added operating work, without addressing changes made before the vote. So the earlier record does not show that S.2 extends that way of treating peaceful critics. This does not show that such incidents have ended.

arguments.title: It supports surveillance used to make criticism of immigration enforcement feel personally threatening.
arguments.pro_html:
Point 6 It supports surveillance used to make criticism of immigration enforcement feel personally threatening.

  • Because S.2 pays for “information technology maintenance and sustainment to support enforcement and removal operations” [1].
  • Because The Brennan Center, a law and policy institute, connects this money to wider surveillance: “The funding will also allow DHS to continue to build surveillance capabilities that facilitate indiscriminate collection of information about Americans as well as immigrants.” [23] DHS is the Department of Homeland Security.
  • Because In March 2026, NPR reported: “Activists and journalists spoke of tactics they felt were intimidating: agents photographing their faces or license plates; calling them by name; or leading them to their homes.” [24]
  • Because NPR did not print one observer's last name because “she fears retaliation from the federal government for speaking out.” [24]

  • Because NPR leaves open how agents got names and addresses. It reports that “privacy advocates say federal agents may be running license plates to access Department of Motor Vehicle data” [24]. That does not show which added resources these encounters depend on.
  • Because The Brennan Center predicts that the money will support “surveillance capabilities that facilitate indiscriminate collection of information about Americans as well as immigrants.” [23] That prediction concerns collecting information. The further claim concerns agents using it to threaten peaceful critics.
  • So This argument joins a broad prediction about collection to encounters whose data source is unknown. It does not show which added capability supports the intimidation.

arguments.title: Added drug scanners strengthen protection against fentanyl poisoning.
arguments.pro_html:
Point 1 Added drug scanners strengthen protection against fentanyl poisoning.

  • Because Section 103 pays for new scanners and for stopping drugs: “Procurement and integration of new nonintrusive inspection equipment” [1] and “combating drug trafficking, including fentanyl and its precursor chemicals” [1]. Nonintrusive inspection equipment scans vehicles without opening them. Precursor chemicals are the ingredients used to make drugs.
  • Because Scanners have helped find hidden fentanyl. In a 2024 vehicle inspection, “CBP officers used non-intrusive technology to screen the sedan revealing anomalies inside all four tires of the vehicle.” [2] (CBP is Customs and Border Protection, the federal border agency.) Officers found packages in the tires: “Four of the packages contained nearly 54,000 blue fentanyl pills” [2].
  • Because These drugs are a hidden, deadly health risk: “Drugs may contain deadly levels of fentanyl, and you wouldn't be able to see it, taste it, or smell it.” [3]
  • So Finding and seizing hidden drugs keeps those drugs out of circulation. Paying for more of this work strengthens protection against a poison in the U.S. drug supply, which serves [NAME]'s wish to protect their health.
arguments.con_html:
Response A successful seizure does not show the drop in fentanyl exposure that this argument gives to more scanners.

  • Because Section 103 pays for “Procurement and integration of new nonintrusive inspection equipment” [1]. Buying equipment and being able to use it are different. The Government Accountability Office (GAO) reported in January 2026: “Some factors have limited the use of the systems, such as limited staff and system outages.” [4]
  • Because Seized fentanyl can be replaced. Jonathan Caulkins explains that synthetic opioids “permit seizures to be replaced in days” [5]. The amount seized does not show how much less fentanyl buyers can get.
  • So Two steps lack support: how this money adds scanning that can really be used, and how added seizures reduce what people are exposed to after suppliers respond. The seized-pill example does not establish the added health protection.

arguments.title: More money for criminal investigations strengthens protection against poisoned pills sold as real medicine.
arguments.pro_html:
Point 2 More money for criminal investigations strengthens protection against poisoned pills sold as real medicine.

  • Because Section 102 pays for Homeland Security Investigations (HSI), the criminal investigation branch of ICE: “to hire, pay, train, and equip Homeland Security Investigations agents and support personnel” [1].
  • Because HSI and its partners have investigated fake pharmacies selling pills made in U.S. drug factories. Their report describes taking pills from those factories: “Law enforcement raided at least three of these pill mills and two other narcotics storage locations, seizing approximately 625,000 counterfeit pills” [6].
  • Because This fraud reaches people seeking health care. The report describes victims “who were in need of medication — people suffering with legitimate ailments.” [6] It reports, “At least nine of the victims later died of narcotics poisoning.” [6]
  • So Added money supports finding these sellers and removing their poisoned pills from sale. That protects people seeking medicine, which gives [NAME] a health reason to favor this added capacity.

Response This argument does not connect its pharmacy case to work that Section 102's limited money may pay for.

  • Because The money must support “functions other than those related to Homeland Security Investigations' immigration enforcement and customs enforcement missions.” [1] Not every activity of Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) is an allowed use of this money. Customs concerns goods crossing the border.
  • Because The case concerns an international drug operation: “Lopez Reyes led the enterprise, orchestrating and controlling every facet of the scheme from the Dominican Republic.” [6] The report also says “the defendants shipped counterfeit pharmaceuticals to victims across the United States and around the world” [6].
  • So Finding pill factories in U.S. basements does not place the investigation outside customs work. This argument names no part of this international case that the limited money would expand outside the excluded missions.

arguments.title: More ability to hold and remove people with violent convictions limits their chances for more attacks.
arguments.pro_html:
Point 3 More ability to hold and remove people with violent convictions limits their chances for more attacks.

  • Because Section 202 pays for enforcement staff and “transportation costs and related costs associated with alien departure or removal operations.” [1] “Removal” means deportation.
  • Because This work includes custody after a criminal sentence ends. ICE (Immigration and Customs Enforcement) reported that it “apprehended an illegally present Dominican national convicted for murder in Massachusetts in 2007 when officers arrested Cesar Augusto Polanco, 59, January 24 at the Massachusetts Correctional Institution in Norfolk after he was released from state custody.” [7]
  • Because ICE kept him in custody for the removal process: “Polanco remains in ICE custody pending removal proceedings.” [7]
  • So Holding people with violent convictions after prison, and removing them, keeps them away from people they could attack here. Added money for staff and transport supports this protection for U.S. residents such as [NAME].
arguments.con_html:
Response One detention does not show that S.2's broader removal money reduces residents' exposure to violence.

  • Because Research on a similar detention and deportation program found, “The results show that the Secure Communities program has had no observable effect on the overall crime rate.” [9] Secure Communities shared local arrest fingerprints with immigration officials.
  • Because A separate study of violent victimization (being a victim of violent crime) in 2005–2014 reports, “The activation of 287(g) jail enforcement agreements and anti-detainer policies had no significant impact on violent victimization risk during the period.” [10]
  • So The example shows one person kept apart from the public. These studies weigh against assuming that more of this enforcement means less violence. They cover older programs and wider crime measures, so they do not settle what would happen with people who have violent convictions.

arguments.title: Supporting transfers from jails makes safer arrests possible.

Point 4 Supporting transfers from jails makes safer arrests possible.

  • Because Section 202 pays for partnerships with state and local police: “Supporting coordination with state and local authorities by expanding, facilitating, and implementing agreements under section 287(g) of the Immigration and Nationality Act” [1].
  • Because One kind of agreement lets trained local officers identify people in jail for immigration proceedings. ICE (Immigration and Customs Enforcement) explains that they “place them into immigration proceedings at the time of release from state or local custody.” [11]
  • Because A transfer can avoid a dangerous arrest in public. In the Polanco case, ICE said cooperation let officers “make the arrest in the safety of a jail cell rather than sending a team of officers into the community to make a potentially dangerous arrest.” [7]
  • So Paying for these partnerships supports more arrests in controlled places. Keeping these confrontations out of public places protects people nearby, which gives [NAME] a separate reason based on personal safety.
arguments.con_html:
Response Expanding 287(g) agreements does not show that jail transfers would replace public arrests.

  • Because These agreements give local officers some immigration powers outside jails too. ICE's February 2026 description says, “The Task Force Model allows your officers to enforce limited immigration authority while performing routine police duties or as an active participant in an ICE-led task force.” [12]
  • Because Section 202 pays for agreements in general. It also pays for “release monitoring, transportation, and arrests of covered unlawful aliens encountered in jurisdictions that are not qualified cooperating jurisdictions” [1].
  • So More authority to make immigration arrests is different from moving the same arrests into jails. This example shows that one transfer was safe. It does not show a change in where arrests happen because of S.2.

arguments.title: Stronger gang investigations protect people from violence in their communities.
arguments.pro_html:
Point 6 Stronger gang investigations protect people from violence in their communities.

  • Because Section 102 pays for agents of Homeland Security Investigations (HSI, the part of ICE that investigates crimes) “to hire, pay, train, and equip” [1]. Section 203 also allows support for state and local crime prevention through “paragraph (3) or (7) of section 100051 of Public Law 119-21” [1]; paragraph (7) of that 2025 law includes “addressing crime and public safety threats” [15].

  • Because A study using national crime-victim survey data from 2005–2014 found a higher risk of being a victim of violent crime: “the activation of Secure Communities and 287(g) task force agreements significantly increased violent victimization risk among Latinos” [10].
  • Because The reporting problem also weakens police protection for the wider public. The president of the Major Cities Chiefs Association explained: “Whether we seek to stop child predators, drug dealers, rapists or robbers – we need the full cooperation of victims and witness. Cooperation is not forthcoming from persons who see their police as immigration agents.” [30]
  • Because A February–March 2026 survey with a random sample of adults in Minneapolis and St. Paul asked about Operation Metro Surge, a large federal immigration deployment. In Minneapolis 49.4% and in St. Paul 46.1% agreed that they were less likely to seek help from police because of how ICE and Border Patrol agents carried it out. These are reported intentions about a federal operation, not measured crime results or an effect of local police working under 287(g). [31]
  • So Paying to expand this police role expands a barrier to reporting crime and helping investigations. [NAME] relies on police being able to find and stop dangerous offenders, so this loss of cooperation gives [NAME] a personal safety reason to oppose S.2.
arguments.con_html:
Response The evidence supports a concern about people seeking help, but it does not show which added local agreements cause a wider loss of protection.

  • Because S.2 pays for local police immigration work through “expanding, facilitating, and implementing agreements under section 287(g)” [1], without choosing between street policing and checks inside jails.
  • Because The older study reports that “our results for 287(g) jail programs showed no significant association with violent victimization risk” [10]. Its results for street policing and Secure Communities showed “no evident impact on victimization risk among non-Latino Whites and Blacks.” [10]
  • Because The study cannot separate reduced trust from other explanations: “The data assembled for our study cannot discern between these potential explanations.” [10] The newer Twin Cities survey reports less willingness to seek police help among adult residents. But it concerns federal agents' conduct during a large surge, ended in March, and does not isolate local police, 287(g) or actual reporting. [31]
  • So These limits narrow the step from older victimization results and reported intentions to added local agreements. They do not answer the concern about seeking help, and they do not show that only Latinos could be affected.

arguments.title: Supporting more detention keeps a route open for infections to reach the wider public.
arguments.pro_html:

  • Because S.2 pays to keep enforcement facilities running: “Funding for facility maintenance and sustainment to support enforcement and removal operations.” [1]

  • Because The CDC's 2019 report records “an additional 33 cases occurred among staff members.” [41] It also records a real response: “IHSC provided >25,000 doses of measles-mumps-rubella (MMR) vaccine in response to mumps in 56 facilities.” [41] IHSC is ICE's health service.

Point 6 It pays for drug detection that could help protect the family setting where parents pass on faith.

  • Because Section 103 pays for inspection equipment to combat “the entry or exit of illicit narcotics” [1] and border work for “combating drug trafficking, including fentanyl and its precursor chemicals” [1]. Precursor chemicals are the ingredients used to make drugs.
  • Because The Government Accountability Office (GAO) explains how the equipment works: “These scans produce images that CBP officers review to help detect illegal drugs or other contraband.” [12] CBP is Customs and Border Protection, the federal border agency.
  • Because Southern Baptists also identify a threat to family life: “Opioid abuse destroys the individual user, but it also destroys the family unit by often separating children from their addicted parents” [13]. Opioids include fentanyl.
  • Because Their statement on the family gives parents the job of passing on faith: “Parents are to teach their children spiritual and moral values and to lead them, through consistent lifestyle example and loving discipline, to make choices based on biblical truth.” [14]

arguments.con_html:

  • Because Finding drugs does not show a lasting loss of supply. Drug-policy researcher Jonathan Caulkins explains the problem: “There is little point in working hard to seize drugs that can be replaced at a very low cost.” [15]
  • Because GAO also says that the Department of Homeland Security's “ability to fully assess the effectiveness of its efforts is limited.” [16]
  • Because The family practice at the end of the chain is teaching faith: “Parents are to teach their children spiritual and moral values” [14].
  • So This argument needs a reason to expect that added detection reduces abuse even though seized drugs can be replaced cheaply. A scanner's ability to reveal hidden items does not supply that step. Without it, this spending is not connected to protecting the family practice of passing on faith.

arguments.title: Added removals put Christians at risk of religious persecution abroad.
arguments.pro_html:
Point 7 Added removals put Christians at risk of religious persecution abroad.

  • Because This danger has already reached Christian converts. In November 2025, the BBC reported a husband's account: “They deported my wife back to Iran even though she is a Christian” [39]. The BBC reported that she had since “been contacted and summoned by Iranian intelligence.” [39]
  • Because The report explains the religious danger: “Converting from Islam is treated as apostasy, and converts face arrest, interrogation and prison terms.” [39] Apostasy means leaving a religion.
  • Because The risk also reaches relatives who go with a deported family member. The joint Christian report warns that this can mean “abandoning the religious freedom that is guaranteed by the U.S. Constitution but is not respected by all countries.” [18]
  • Because Southern Baptists' 2011 religious liberty resolution affirms the freedom “to worship without harassment or impediment from the state” [40] and calls for prayer for Christians “persecuted, imprisoned, or facing execution for their testimony of faith in Jesus.” [40]
  • So More ability to remove people supports a system that has returned Christians to danger and puts the worship of relatives who go with them at risk. Keeping their freedom to live by their faith gives [NAME] a reason to oppose S.2.
arguments.con_html:
Response The persecution evidence does not connect S.2's transport money to more unsafe returns, because the law and other decisions control where people are sent.

  • Because The BBC reports that Ali's wife was returned to Iran and summoned by Iranian intelligence. Her lawyer said sensitive information about her change of religion and other reasons for asking for protection “was not removed before deportation.” [39] This account concerns how protection, destinations and religious information were handled.
  • Because Existing law bars removal to a country when the official finds this kind of threat, with listed exceptions: “the Attorney General may not remove an alien to a country if the Attorney General decides that the alien's life or freedom would be threatened in that country because of the alien's race, religion, nationality, membership in a particular social group, or political opinion.” [41]
  • Because The family report's warning about relatives depends on the destination: “abandoning the religious freedom that is guaranteed by the U.S. Constitution but is not respected by all countries.” [18] Section 202's transport money does not choose destinations or replace decisions about protection.
  • So More removal money alone does not show more returns to religious persecution, including for relatives who move with a deported family member. This does not show that unsafe returns will not happen; the BBC case shows that one did.
